label: Lies, jokes and complaints
rationale: What friends say to each other: lies, jokes, complaints, venting and secrets.
mixUps: Lying takes tsuku (uso tsuita), but joking, complaining and venting take iu. monku o iu is complaining at someone or about something wrong, while guchi o iu is grumbling to let off steam. naisho takes ni suru, not mamoru.

targets.verbSense: let out (breath); in speech it survives mainly in uso o tsuku and tameiki o tsuku (sigh)
targets.trap: English 'tell' leads to uso o iu, which natives also say (uso bakkari itte, uso iwanaide), but the set phrase for lying is uso o tsuku: uso tsuita, uso tsukanaide.
targets.use: Heard as denial or accusation: uso tsuitenai yo (I'm not lying), uso tsukanaide (don't lie to me). Bare uso! is the 'no way!' reaction, not an accusation.

example.romaji: uso tsuitenai yo, honto da yo.
example.ja: 嘘ついてないよ、ほんとだよ。

examplePolite.romaji: uso wa tsuitemasen. hontou desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 嘘はついてません。本当ですよ。

targets.trap: English 'make a joke' leads to joudan o tsukuru, which doesn't work; jokes are said (joudan o iu), and 'just kidding' is joudan da yo.
targets.use: Heard in teasing: mata joudan itte (there you go joking again), joudan itteru dake (I'm only joking). The short replies joudan da yo (just kidding) and joudan desho? (you're kidding, right?) leave the verb out. joudan ja nai yo is the annoyed opposite: this is no joke / you've got to be kidding me.

example.ja: 冗談言ってるだけだよ。

examplePolite.romaji: joudan o itteru dake desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 冗談を言ってるだけですよ。

targets.trap: English has one verb, 'complain'; Japanese says the complaint: monku o iu, not monku suru. Dictionary picks sound formal: kujou o iu is lodging a complaint with a landlord or company, fuhei o iu is bookish, and kureemu (from 'claim') is a customer complaint to a business. Venting about your day is guchi o iu.
targets.use: Heard mostly as a rebuke: monku iwanaide (stop complaining), monku bakkari (always complaining). Complaining to a shop or a neighbour is also monku o iu, and being on the receiving end is monku iwareta (someone complained to me). Casual speech often drops o.
targets.notes: monku aru? (got a problem with that?) is the confrontational retort, and monku nai yo (no complaints, fine by me) the easy-going reply; both belong to monku ga aru.

example.ja: 文句ばっかり言わないでよ。

examplePolite.ja: 文句ばかり言わないでください。

targets.use: Venting about work, family or your lot, usually to a friend over a drink: guchi itte gomen (sorry for moaning), guchi bakkari (always moaning). The listener's side is guchi o kiku (guchi nara kiku yo), and guchiru is the one-word casual verb. monku o iu is objecting to someone or something; guchi is letting off steam about your situation.
targets.notes: guchi o kobosu means the same and sounds a little more literary.

example.ja: ごめん、愚痴ばっかり言って。
example.english: Sorry, all I do is moan.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、愚痴ばかり言ってしまって。

targets.verbSense: do; with ni, make something into X (kore ni suru = I'll take this one)
targets.trap: English 'keep a secret' leads to mamoru. himitsu o mamoru is fine (himitsu mamotte ne works too), but naisho doesn't take mamoru: 'keep this between us' is naisho ni shite (or himitsu ni shite).
targets.use: Almost always a request: kore naisho ni shite ne (keep this between us). On its own, naisho da yo means 'it's a secret' when you won't tell.
targets.notes: himitsu ni suru is the neutral twin.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa naisho ni shite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: これは内緒にしてくださいね。

reviewPool.english: wake up (from sleep); feel wide awake (me ga sameta)
get into bed, get under the covers
